picked.t: Hanoi restaurant with 100 home-cooked dishes recognized by Michelin
picked.body: The restaurant on Phan Dinh Phung Street in Ba Dinh Ward offers its guests traditional family recipes from grandmothers and mothers. The name "Mammom" comes from two ideas: "mom" and "mam mam", a sound Vietnamese people use for eating delicious food. The restaurant received the Michelin Guide 2026 Bib Gourmand, a distinction recognizing restaurants that serve high-quality food at great value, within two years of its opening in June 2024. Behind the 100-dish menu is 35-year-old head chef Ha Van Tinh. He has 15 years of culinary experience and spent a lot of time studying food culture and ingredients across Vietnam. Every year, he travels around the country to explore local ingredients, food trends, and regional cooking styles, and brings these experiences into his menu. The Michelin award serves as strong motivation for him to keep researching ingredients, creating new recipes, and improving his skills. After the Michelin recognition, the number of Vietnamese guests visiting Mammom has risen by 50%. It used to mainly serve foreign tourists, especially the U.S., Europe, and Northeast Asia. The restaurant spans six floors, and has a floor area of 220 square meters. It opens for lunch from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. and dinner from 5:30 p.m. to 10 p.m. Mammom can seat up to 300 guests at a time and serves around 600 a day. On average, a meal costs between VND200,000-300,000 (US$8-11) per person. For first-time visitors, recommended dishes include crab spring rolls (pictured), glazed pork ribs with garlic fish sauce, steamed squid with cilantro fish sauce, and beef salad with eggplant. The menu offers comforting, home-cooked flavors, featuring braised fish, stir-fried vegetables, caramelized pork belly, and grilled ribs. The space is elegant yet simple, giving one the feeling of enjoying a family meal. Every day except Monday, the restaurant has live traditional music performances from 6 p.m. to 8 p.m. On international platforms like Tripadvisor, the restaurant has been acclaimed, earning a rating of 4.9 out of 5 stars. Marien, a British tourist who visited in May, liked the service because the staff spoke fluent English. They clearly explained how to enjoy each dish and even suggested local sightseeing spots in Hanoi. Thao Nguyen, a resident of Ha Dong Ward in Hanoi, learned about the restaurant after its Michelin recognition. She shared that while the prices are quite high, the food quality is "beyond fault." picked.t: 25-year-old restaurant chain Crystal Jade closes 3 Singapore outlets in one month, 5 so far this year
picked.body: Crystal Jade recently confirmed to The Straits Times that its Hong Kong Kitchen outlet at The Clementi Mall had closed on Tuesday while its Jurong Point location is set to cease operations on Friday as part of its ongoing outlet network review. The group had closed another local outlet at the Great World shopping mall on Sept. 1 and two others earlier this year, citing the same reason, as reported by AsiaOne . Established in Singapore in 1991, Crystal Jade grew over the years and opened more than 100 outlets globally across several dining concepts in Singapore and overseas markets, including China, South Korea and Vietnam. Its operations in the city-state comprise six restaurant brands, ranging from Cantonese fine dining to casual noodle, dim sum and other Chinese cuisine concepts. Its Crystal Jade Golden Palace outlet at The Paragon mall was awarded one Michelin star from 2016 to 2018. Following the latest closures, Crystal Jade has 13 Singapore outlets, including four Hong Kong Kitchen restaurants, according to its website. The shutdowns add to the growing list of food and beverage closures in Singapore this year, with 2,101 such businesses shutting down in the first seven months, a 25.1% year-on-year increase, according to data from the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority. Data released by the Singapore Department of Statistics earlier this month shows F&B services sales fell 1.9% year-on-year to an estimated S$1.6 billion in July, following a 2.3% decline in June. Food courts and other eating places, as well as cafes, saw the biggest declines of 6.6% and 6.4%, respectively, while fast-food outlets and food caterers reported sales growth.

picked.t: Vietnamese student gives up Western plans to follow his sister to 'China's MIT'
picked.body: Nguyen Khoa Vu, a graduate of Hanoi's Foreign Language Specialized School, has won a 50% tuition scholarship to Tsinghua University's Zhishan College. Tsinghua, often dubbed "China's MIT", ranks 14th in the QS World University Rankings 2027. Zhishan, a social sciences college Tsinghua launched in 2024, charges CNY26,000 (US$3,900) a year in tuition. Its majors include economics, sociology, political science and public administration, international politics and statistics. Vu's older sister, Nguyen Vu Tue Giang, was admitted to Tsinghua on a scholarship in 2025. Used to Western culture and passionate about basketball, Vu flatly refused when his mother suggested he follow his sister to Beijing. "At one point I told my parents straight out: "either the U.K. or the U.S., or I stay home," he recalled. In August 2025, he traveled to Beijing with his family for his sister's enrollment. The modern classrooms, swimming pool and basketball courts, along with time spent with Vietnamese students there, won him over. "Everything felt right, and I realized this was the environment for me," he said. Vu's application included his transcripts, language certificates, recommendation letters, a personal essay and a self-introduction video. He also submitted math and Chinese results from the China Scholastic Competency Assessment (CSCA), a new standardized test for international undergraduate applicants. He kept an average above 9 out of 10 throughout high school. His language scores include IELTS 7.5 and HSK 6, the highest of the Chinese proficiency test's six core levels. In his essay, Vu wrote about setting aside his dream of playing professional basketball to focus on academics and economics. "I wanted to show that however passionate I am about sports, I can set it aside and excel at another goal," he said. "A sports career is a huge challenge because it requires substantial resources and the right environment to develop," he added. He picked economics because he inherited his mother's head for business, he said. While still in school, he imported trendy toys and sold sneakers online. After clearing the application review, Vu advanced to an in-person interview. Three professors spent 15 minutes questioning him on a range of topics and even had him solve math problems on the spot. Candidates must keep the interview content confidential. "At one point I admitted I didn't know anything about a topic the professor raised and asked for a different question," Vu said, crediting honesty for his success. Vu handled pressure remarkably well, moving from HSK 4 to HSK 6 in six months, said Hoang Lan Chi, a lecturer at Hanoi's University of Languages and International Studies who guided him through the application. "Vu proved he meets the university's admission criteria. He is well-rounded, from academics, music and sports to determination, perseverance and discipline," she said. Giang, self-motivated and a natural student, mostly needed support from the sidelines, said their mother, Mai Dung. Vu was capable but sometimes distracted, she said, so she watched him more closely, often pointing to successful role models and steering him toward his sister's example. "I let my children experience things, take responsibility and face failure early, while quietly creating situations that spark their passion," she said. She believes that bringing Vu along to his sister's enrollment, and letting him mingle with Tsinghua students, helped him find his own goal.
